summary.title: The Ultimate Code Kata
summary.one_liner: Learn why daily work isn't enough to grow as a programmer, and how deliberate "effortful study" through code kata drills, Norvig's advice, and blogging or open source work can build real skill.
keywords: how to get better at programming
peter norvig teach yourself programming in ten years
takeaways: Doing your job every day is not the same as deliberate practice; growth comes from tackling problems just beyond your current ability.
Steve Yegge's practice drills include writing a skills self-assessment, reading good and bad code, reviewing resumes, and sitting in on technical interviews.
Peter Norvig recommends talking to programmers, reading others' code, taking classes, maintaining others' code, learning unfamiliar languages, and understanding hardware costs.
The author's own kata are writing a blog and actively contributing to notable open source projects, since actions are judged more than words.
summary.summary: The author builds on Steve Yegge's 2005 essay on practice, arguing that repeated experience alone does not make someone an expert, citing Ericsson's research on effortful study at the edge of one's ability. He lists Yegge's practice drills (such as reviewing resumes, reading code, and sitting in on interviews), Peter Norvig's recommendations for learning programming, and links to Pragmatic Dave's 21 code katas and coding dojos. The post ends with the author's two personal kata: writing a blog and contributing to open source projects.
